papers.title: scOnion: Cross-Modal Concordance-Aware Joint Analysis of Cells and Features in Single-Cell Multiomic Data
papers.abstract: Single-cell multiomic assays jointly profile gene expression and chromatin accessibility in the same cells, enabling direct analysis of cross-layer coordination. However, agreement between modalities varies across cells, and existing integration methods often emphasize shared structure, potentially averaging away cell-specific cross-modal discordance that carries biological signal. Here we present scOnion, a concordance-aware computational framework that quantifies cross-modality agreement and propagates this information into downstream analyses. Starting from paired low-rank representations obtained by spectral integration, scOnion computes per-cell concordance scores, a concordance-aware joint cell embedding, and an induced cross-modal feature embedding. The cell embedding preserves structure strongly represented in either modality, improving cell-type and state resolution, while the feature embedding scores candidate regulatory element(rE)-to-gene (rE2G) pairs. Across immune, neural, and developmental functional genomic datasets, scOnion's concordance patterns are reproducible and cell-resolved, with low-concordance cells enriched for modality-specific structure. scOnion also prioritizes candidate rE2G pairs, including distal links, with stronger support from external Hi-C contacts and fine-mapped eQTL data than the baseline linkage methods. In a B-cell fate bifurcation study, scOnion reveals remodeling of concordance and rE2G coupling during lineage commitment. scOnion embeds ~70,000 cells and computes rE2G links on CPU in 30 minutes, extends naturally to other multiomic assays such as CITE-seq, and is available as open-source software.

papers.title: Heterogeneous Effects Across Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) Driver Mutations Challenges a Unified Model of CHIP
papers.abstract: Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is an age-associated expansion of hematopoietic stem cells harboring somatic mutations in the absence of overt malignancy. CHIP driver genes impart divergent effects on many biological processes, yet the mechanisms underlying these gene-specific effects, particularly in non-hematologic disease contexts, remain poorly understood. We analyzed 466 samples from the Multi-Ancestry Genomics, Epigenomics, and Transcriptomics of Alzheimer's Disease dataset, and identified function-specific differences between CHIP categorizations. Uniquely, DNMT3A CHIP was associated with global hypomethylation, STAG2 CHIP increased mutation burden, HSC differentiation CHIP strongly triggered adaptive immune response, and proliferative signaling CHIP induced coagulation and cell adhesion. These divergent functions differentially modulate inflammatory pathways and suggest investigating CHIP's downstream effects through a driver gene function-based approach rather than treating CHIP as a single entity. Our multi-omics analyses provide such a framework to improve mechanistic interpretation of conflicting relationships between CHIP and diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

papers.title: Structural and functional reference maps of transcriptional enhancers in the developing human cortex
papers.abstract: Non-coding regulatory variation is the major driver of human phenotypic diversity, yet maps of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their variability across developmental cell types remain limited. Here, we integrated single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from 54 mid-gestation human prenatal cortical donors to generate a CRE atlas comprising 1,165,697 candidate CREs across 104,266 cortical nuclei. Chromatin-state annotation classified 1.5% of CREs as bivalent promoters, 0.3% as active promoters, 39.8% as active distal enhancers, 1.3% as CTCF-associated insulators but 57.1% remain unresolved. Overlap with an external enhancer assay dataset showed that many unresolved CREs, nevertheless, exhibit regulatory activity; thus, current chromatin signatures underestimate the functional regulatory landscape. Pseudo-bulk analysis across major cortical lineages revealed that the prenatal cortical regulome is dominated by lineage-restricted CREs, with only a small core shared across all lineages. Restricted CREs were enriched for unresolved elements, intermediate-sharing classes were enhancer-dominant, and broadly shared CREs showed the strongest promoter-proximal and bivalent contribution. Lineage-selective transcription factor (TF) sequence grammar analyses identified progenitor-associated homeodomain programs and neuronal basic helix-loop-helix signatures, together with representative candidate regulators such as SOX10, NFIA, EMX2, DLX1, ARX, and RFX3. Across donors, developmental time, and sex, prenatal cortical CREs segregated into a stable versus variable regulatory compartments. Broadly, recurrent and developmentally persistent CREs had greater activity, on average, and greater enrichment for promoter-associated states, whereas donor-restricted and temporally restricted CREs had lower activity and were enriched for unresolved and enhancer-like elements. Sex-biased CREs were rare but highly specific: female-biased CREs were predominantly X-linked, broadly shared, and developmentally persistent, whereas male-biased CREs were more numerous, less resolved, and more restricted across lineage and developmental contexts. Together, these results define the prenatal cortical regulatory landscape at single-cell resolution, revealing a small, stable, promoter-rich core and a larger variable, enhancer- and unresolved-rich compartment in which lineage diversification is driven primarily by selective deployment of distal regulatory elements.

papers.title: Genomic variation of Dutch traditional cattle breeds captured in a Dutch cattle pangenome
papers.abstract: Traditional livestock breeds are reservoirs of genetic variation lost elsewhere by selection for productivity, yet are rarely represented in reference genome resources. Traditional cattle (Bos taurus) in the Netherlands are severely endangered, with some populations having declined by up to 95 % between 2020 and 2026. We generated 12 assemblies from seven traditional Dutch breeds and combined them with a Holstein Friesian assembly and the Hereford cattle reference to build the first Dutch cattle pangenome (2 881 293 997 bp), a graph containing 193.4 Mb of sequence absent from the international reference. More than 80 % of this sequence was breed private, and this fraction rose with variant size to 99 % for segments of at least one kilobase. Genotyping 54 short-read sequenced animals of these Dutch breeds against the graph recovered 55 865 structural variants and resolved four genetic clusters. The Groningen White Headed was the most differentiated breed while carrying the lowest nucleotide diversity, whereas the recently derived Improved Red and Deep Red remained close to their Meuse-Rhine-Yssel progenitor. Holstein Friesian formed no cluster of its own and contributed the least amount of novel sequence, a reflection of its historical use in upgrading traditional breeds. Ten structural variants located within genes were fixed within a single breed and ranked among the most breed-differentiated of all 55 865 SVs by VST , including a 174 bp deletion in KIT in the Dutch Belted. Pangenomes recover breed-defining variation that linear references cannot represent, supporting conservation and selection in traditional cattle.

papers.title: Differential gene expression profiling of lumbar disc degeneration in the RuDDS cohort
papers.abstract: Lumbar disc degeneration disease (LDDD) is a major structural cause of low back pain, one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, and has no disease-modifying treatment. We performed RNA sequencing of 72 intraoperative intervertebral disc samples from the Russian disc degeneration study (RuDDS) cohort, comparing severe (Pfirrmann grades IV-V) with moderate (grade III) degeneration. We identified 731 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 347 upregulated and 384 downregulated in severely degenerated discs) in the 57 samples that passed quality control. Upregulated DEGs were enriched for extracellular matrix organisation, ossification, and TGF-beta; and Hippo signalling, whereas downregulated DEGs were enriched for immune and inflammatory processes. We identified five differentially active transcription factors, including the TGF-beta; effectors SMAD3 and SMAD4 and the osteogenic regulator DLX5. Of the five, only DLX5 was also a DEG. DEGs were enriched for LDDD-associated genes from Open Targets (odds ratio = 1.68, P = 3.37 * 10-6). Connectivity mapping against the LINCS L1000 database showed that histone deacetylase inhibitors and glucocorticoids reverse the signature of severe degeneration. Together, these results point to TGF-beta-driven fibrotic and osteogenic remodelling as the dominant transcriptional feature of severe disc degeneration, and prioritise candidate genes and compounds for functional validation.

papers.title: Functional interrogation of osteoarthritis-associated regulatory variants and effector genes.
papers.abstract: Background: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with osteoarthritis (OA); however, the regulatory variants and effector genes underlying most associations remain unresolved. Results: We used complementary functional genomic approaches in chondrocytes to resolve prioritized OA risk loci. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) in primary human chondrocytes identified allele-specific regulatory activity at variants across multiple loci, two of which were independently validated using low-throughput reporter assays. In parallel, integration of OA GWAS signals with chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac CUT&Tag, and chromatin conformation data prioritised candidate regulatory elements for CRISPR based perturbation. CRISPR activation and interference supported functional regulatory relationships between OA risk regions and Pappalysin 1 (PAPPA) and Sprouty RTK signaling antagonist 4 (SPRY4) as target genes. At the 9q33 locus, multiple independent lines of evidence converged on rs1895062, which resides in an accessible region that loops to the PAPPA promoter. The OA risk G allele at rs1895062 results in higher regulatory activity by MPRA and low throughput reporter assay. Activation of this region by CRISPR increases PAPPA gene expression and induces widespread transcriptional changes involving extracellular matrix remodelling and other OA-relevant pathways. Conclusion: Integrating genetic association, genomic and epigenomic data, and functional perturbation in disease-relevant cells can resolve the regulatory mechanisms underlying OA risk loci. Using this multi-faceted approach, we provide convergent functional evidence for rs1895062 as a likely causal variant that controls PAPPA gene expression and OA risk.

papers.title: Clonal landscape of human nephrons
papers.abstract: The nephron is a highly compartmentalized structure, where distinct patterns of somatic mosaicism may be established and contribute to altered kidney functions with aging. Here we show extensive remodeling of aged nephrons by mosaic clones using integrated sequencing of >1,000 microdissected samples collected from anatomically distinct nephron segments. Striking differences were observed across segments. Proximal tubules exhibited markedly higher mutation burdens with mutational signatures characteristic of clear cell renal cell carcinoma and larger clonal expansion than other segments. Cancer-related mutations were observed only infrequently and largely limited to proximal tubules, while copy number abnormalities were quite common, most frequently involving chromosomes 18, 10, 7, X, 22, 3 and 9, in a segment-specific manner. Clone size appears to depend more on cell turnover than on driver events. Particularly, in collecting ducts, numerous clones independently acquiring chromosome 18 loss evolved over years and ultimately replaced 15-47% of collecting duct cells in aged donors despite minimal increase in their clone size, likely reflecting strong fitness advantage of chromosome 18-deficient clones under slow tissue turnover. Chromosome 18-deficient cells significantly correlated with fibrosis and showed reduced expression of chromosome 18 genes, including those involved in sodium handling (NEDD4L) and TGF-{beta} signaling (SMAD2/4/7). In line with this, GSEA of chromosome 18-deficient cells revealed enhanced hallmark pathways overlapping those associated with acute kidney injury that are related to TGF-{beta} signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and inflammatory responses. These findings illustrate how nephrons are remodeled with aging, providing insights into the role of somatic remodelling in altered kidney structures and functions with aging.

papers.title: Alternative splicing edits intrinsically disordered regions across human protein isoforms
papers.abstract: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) lack a stable three-dimensional structure, yet they mediate many of the interactions and regulatory functions of proteins. Alternative splicing produces multiple protein isoforms from a single gene, and because individual exons can encode all or part of an IDR, splicing has the potential to add, remove or reshape disordered regions. However, it remains unclear whether splicing preferentially acts on disordered sequence in all kinds of proteins, how it changes an IDR from one isoform to another, and how this relationship arose during evolution. Here, we map predicted disorder onto the coding exons and genomic codons of human protein isoforms, which allows any two isoforms of a gene to be compared directly, and analyze this map across protein classes and families. We find that alternatively spliced exons are more disordered than constitutive exons in every class of protein, from transcription factors to metabolic enzymes, and that splicing usually changes IDRs at their ends, adding or removing disordered segments as modular units rather than cutting through them. The disordered sequence that splicing varies is compositionally distinct from the disorder that all isoforms share. Notably, the apparent loss of disorder over gene evolution reflects differences between protein families rather than change within them, whereas exons whose splice sites are conserved in few mammals encode more disorder than the other exons of the same gene, with a composition resembling that of young genes. Our results suggest that alternative splicing treats intrinsic disorder as a modular, evolvable layer of protein architecture, and that exons with poorly conserved splice sites may be one route by which disordered sequence enters proteins.

papers.title: No evidence of genome-wide selection against sensetranscription starts in human introns
papers.abstract: RNA polymerase II often starts transcription inside genes, usually at elements that initiate in both directions. An intragenic start pointing in the gene's direction (a sense start) makes RNA that passes the gene's splice sites and polyadenylation signals and may interfere with the gene. Introns may therefore have lost sequences that start sense transcription. In PRO-cap data from K562 and HCT116 cells, the sense start at intronic elements, measured against the antisense start, is a fifth to a third weaker than at intergenic elements of similar read depth. Sequence models that have never seen an element's chromosome predict 30-42% of this bias from local DNA, except models trained on K562 applied to HCT116. However, introns as a whole show little or no depletion of predicted sense starts, and among 76,215 human genomes, variants predicted to create sense starts are not kept rarer than those creating antisense starts. In both cell lines, and in K562 GRO-cap data, strong measured start sites are rarer on the gene strand, mainly near the 5'' end of active genes. Thus, weaker sense starts appear to be a feature of individual active elements, partly predictable from their sequence, and we find no sign that selection has removed such sequences from introns.

papers.title: Transcription starting inside human introns is widespread but mostly yields short-lived RNA
papers.abstract: Background: Thousands of annotated long non-coding RNAs lie inside introns of protein-coding genes, on the host's strand, but whether they are independent genes or pieces of host transcripts is usually unknown. An independent gene needs its own start site. Results: We mapped transcription starts inside introns, using nascent capped RNA from two human cell lines. The approach detected the start sites of 94% of clearly expressed protein-coding genes nested in introns and confirmed 1,346 and 3,061 intronic start sites, almost all unannotated. Most are cell-type-specific, carrying active chromatin marks and motifs of the cell's key transcription factors. Many initiate as strongly as the hosts' alternative promoters but rarely sustain transcription: after a synchronised restart of transcription, their nascent RNA fades within a few kilobases, their short transcripts are partly degraded by the nuclear exosome, and the sequence downstream rarely has the early splice-donor site that protects promoter transcripts. Per initiation event, they leave about as little stable RNA as start sites between genes, so host transcription does not explain their low output. Expressed intronic RNAs on the host's strand more often lack their own start site than those on the opposite strand. Conclusions: Transcription starting inside human introns is widespread but mostly yields short-lived RNA. Many intronic long non-coding RNAs on the host's strand are therefore likely to be pieces of host transcripts rather than independent genes, which matters for their annotation. All intronic start sites in both cell lines, with every measure used here, are provided as a resource.

papers.title: Population genomics of the Anopheles farauti complex reveals a distinct regime of malaria vector evolution in the southwest Pacific
papers.abstract: Abstract: The southwest Pacific has one of the highest per-capita malaria burdens outside Africa, yet how its malaria mosquitoes evolve is largely unknown. In African vectors, insecticide resistance evolves rapidly in large, connected populations carrying abundant standing variation. Southwest Pacific vectors show little to no biochemical resistance despite decades of insecticide-based control. We analyse 495 genomes from six taxa of the Anopheles farauti complex, which includes the region's major vectors. The complex radiated rapidly in the late Pleistocene concomitant to the peopling of Near Oceania. Thereafter, post-glacial sea-level rise and climate change fragmented its populations into recently colonised island isolates. Successive environmental and colonisation bottlenecks left a legacy of extraordinary inbreeding, most marked in island populations of the coastal specialist An. farauti sensu stricto, where sustained low effective population size has allowed deleterious alleles to be purged effectively; the inland generalists An. hinesorum and An. oreios retain more variation. After five decades of chemical control we recover a single resistance sweep, at Gste2, alongside recent selection at species-specific chemosensory gene repertoires. Severe inbreeding and the loss of standing variation have not prevented ecological success, challenging assumptions about how much variation and connectivity a vector population needs to thrive. This work establishes the first genomic foundation for this major vector system of endemic species through a biogeographically diverse region of the world.

papers.title: Evolutionary rescue of rare human genetic disorders in yeast models
papers.abstract: Several thousand human disease-associated genes have clear yeast orthologs, making yeast an ideal model system for advancing a basic understanding of human disease. We used CRISPR-Cas9 editing to generate 51 yeast strains with 11 human disease-associated variants, focusing on human disease genes involved in protein glycosylation, ribosome maturation, mitochondrial function, and RNA regulation. We find that most of these alleles recapitulate as fitness defects in yeast. To enrich for suppressors, we evolved these populations for 1,000 generations and performed whole genome sequencing. We identified both known and previously unknown suppressor mutations. For example, we identify mutations in DPM1 and RPS9B that compensate for disease phenotypes of ALG7 and SDO1, respectively. Reconstructed strains harboring evolved suppressor mutations and the original disease alleles demonstrate that these suppressors rescue fitness and may compensate for defects in molecular function. By exerting continuous selective pressure over thousands of generations, experimental evolution allows us to select for suppressor mutations, including those with modest fitness effects or occurring at lower frequencies, which are underrepresented in traditional genetic screens. Our results map local genetic interaction networks centered around disease-associated alleles, providing greater insights into disease phenotypes and informing potential targeted therapies for disease management in patients with rare disorders.

papers.title: ModFormer: A unified structure-aware model of transcriptome-wide A-to-I RNA editing
papers.abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing can recode transcripts without permanently altering the genome. ADAR-catalyzed editing depends on both local sequence and RNA secondary structure, making it difficult to anticipate which sites will be edited or how mutations will change their activity. Moving from observing endogenous A-to-I editing to using it as a programmable molecular tool requires predicting how editing responds to sequence changes. Here, we present ModFormer, a model that integrates RNA sequence representations with predicted secondary structure to predict ADAR-mediated editing. Trained on human data, ModFormer predicts editing sites and rates across substrates and species unseen during training, recovers established sequence and pairing preferences, and anticipates experimentally measured responses to RNA mutations. These predictions prioritize responsive sites in mutational screens and guide an autonomous AI agent toward candidate RNA designs. ModFormer provides a framework for predicting how sequence changes reshape RNA editing and can be adapted to new substrates with limited experimental data.

papers.title: Annotated reference genome for the Critically Endangered, paleoendemic Bermuda skink (Plestiodon longirostris)
papers.abstract: Skinks, one of the largest vertebrate families with over 1,500 described species, are represented by only 19 publicly available chromosome-level genome assemblies. Here, we present the first whole-genome assembly of the Bermuda skink, Plestiodon longirostris, a Critically Endangered, evolutionarily distinct, and endemic species. We conducted a de novo genome assembly using Oxford Nanopore Technology long reads, followed by reference-guided scaffolding against the five-lined skink Plestiodon fasciatus and Gilberts skink Plestiodon gilberti genomes. We generated a 1.496 Gb assembly with 2,579 scaffold contigs over 500 bp in length, a scaffold N50 of 224.1 Mb, with 98.7% Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) completeness score and 94.8% of gene annotations transferred from the P. fasciatus annotated genome. Repetitive elements comprised 48.37% of the genome, including 33.79% unclassified repeats, while 9% of transposable element sequences contained internal stop codons, consistent with other reptile genomes. Synteny analysis revealed strong conservation of macrochromosomes and gene order through the Plestiodon genus, and progressive chromosomal rearrangement with increased phylogenetic distance across the wider skink family. We also present the first mitogenome for the species. These genomic resources will further evolutionary research in the skink family and will facilitate applied conservation genomic approaches in this Critically Endangered species.

papers.title: Full-length transcript architecture reveals RNA fate and regulatory state
papers.abstract: Pervasive transcription generates diverse RNAs, including promoter-upstream transcripts (PROMPTs), coding and non-coding transcripts from protein-coding loci, and enhancer RNAs. How their full-length architectures relate to RNA fate remains poorly understood. Using ultra-deep sequencing of polyadenylated and non-polyadenylated capped RNAs from mouse embryonic stem cells, we show that nuclear exosome surveillance of PROMPTs is associated with transcript length and sequence composition. We show that for most protein-coding genes, capped transcripts are dominated by cytosolic 3'[->]5' degradation intermediates or premature transcription termination products rather than full-length mRNAs. The relative abundance of intact mRNAs, cytosolic degradation intermediates and prematurely terminated transcripts varies between genes and is associated with gene architecture, expression level and biological function. Finally, we identify a class of convergently transcribed enhancers enriched for Polycomb repressive complex 2-associated proteins and poised enhancer features, with an increased propensity for activation during differentiation. Full-length transcript architecture thus reveals RNA fate and regulatory state.

papers.title: The 'near T2T' Canton-S assembly is inconsistent with other Canton-S genomes
papers.abstract: Canton-S is among the most widely used Drosophila melanogaster strains, underlying substantial community infrastructure, including serving as a wild-type strain for: genetics studies; studying phenotypes, especially in behavioral studies; and complex trait mapping studies among many others. The recent 'near T2T' assembly of Canton-S (LIU et al.) is presented as delivering modern sequencing and assembly quality to the Drosophila community via this important strain. I find that this assembly is inconsistent with three other independently sequenced Canton-S genome assemblies on a magnitude comparable to differences between distinct strains, raising concerns about its genetic identity that the community should consider when choosing whether to adopt it as a resource.

papers.title: Large-scale analyses of short open reading frames yield few if any novel human genes
papers.abstract: Recent efforts to discover new protein-coding genes in the human genome have yielded a large number of short open reading frames supported by limited experimental evidence supporting translational activity in fragmented parts of those sequences. We examined the 19 highest-confidence predictions made by the TransCODE Consortium, and found that three of them were previously known and thus not novel, while the other 16 could be explained by mechanisms that do not require the assertion of a novel human protein. In several cases, the alternative explanations for the other 16 had already been published. We also analyzed the other 118 predictions and found that most of these, too, could be explained without positing the existence of novel proteins. Our findings show that in the search for new human genes, evidence of transcription and translation can almost always be explained by known mechanisms, and that the predictions of the TransCODE Consortium likely do not include any novel genes.

papers.title: Somatic mutation detection from non-malignant liver tissues using cell-free DNA
papers.abstract: Somatic mutations accumulate in the liver during aging, yet their role in chronic liver disease (CLD) remains unclear due to the difficulty of obtaining liver tissue for analysis. Here, we demonstrate that circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) can be used as a minimally invasive tool to detect liver-derived somatic mutations in patients with CLD. Using ultra-deep targeted duplex sequencing, we show that CLD patients have a higher mutation burden in CLD-associated somatic mutation (CASM) genes compared to healthy individuals. Recurrent driver mutations, including CHD4, INSR, and GPAM, were detected in both liver tissue and cfDNA, with distinct mutational patterns linked to disease etiology: INSR mutations were enriched in metabolic-dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease, while GPAM mutations were associated with alcohol-related liver disease. Liver transplantation led to a significant reduction in CASM mutation burden in cfDNA, providing strong evidence for the diseased-liver origin of these mutations. These findings establish cfDNA analysis as a scalable and noninvasive platform for investigating somatic evolution in non-malignant tissues, offering new opportunities for molecular stratification, longitudinal monitoring, and early detection of CLD progression.

papers.title: Distinctive fragmentation of circulating DNA from chromosome Y and its alteration in cancer
papers.abstract: Circulating cell-free DNA (cirDNA) fragmentation reflects chromatin organization and represents a promising source of cancer biomarkers. Here, we characterized the fragmentation patterns and nucleosome occupancy of Y chromosome (chrY) cirDNA in healthy individuals and cancer patients. In healthy males, we found that the shorter chrY-derived cirDNA fragments predominantly originate from heterochromatic regions. We also observed substantially lower nucleosome occupancy on chrY than on all other chromosomes, a finding independently supported by micrococcal nuclease digestion data. Remarkably, in patients with colorectal, pancreatic, lung and prostate cancer, the chrY-specific enrichment of shorter fragments was markedly attenuated, contrasting with the increased fragmentation usually observed in cancer when chromosome specificity is disregarded. We reproduced these observations in an independent local cohort of healthy and colorectal cancer patients. We could exploit ratios of short (100-147 bp) to long (147-200 bp) fragments between chrY and other chromosomes to discriminate healthy males from patients with colorectal, pancreatic, and lung cancers with AUCs above 0.98. Autosomes 19, 17, and 22 also displayed atypical fragment patterns, different from chrY and associated with gene density. This last observation was confirmed in females.

papers.title: High prevalence and diversity of nematodes associated with Europe's most destructive forest pest, revealed by off-target genomic data
papers.abstract: We know very little about the biotic interactions of most species on our planet, including many organisms that play a crucial role in ecosystem networks. One highly cost-effective way of reconstructing these networks is to analyse the rapidly growing collections of high-throughput sequencing datasets. In this study, we examine a large whole-genome resequencing dataset for the spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus), one of Europe's most destructive forest pests, to determine the diversity and distribution of associated organisms that such datasets can reveal. We found that from among metagenomic datasets for 312 adult beetles from across the species' European range, 69% contained small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA) reads from other eukaryotic organisms, most often nematodes. Among 13 rRNA-reconstructed nematode species, Contortylenchus sp. and Micoletzkya sp. were the most prevalent taxa across the European populations. Frequently, nematode DNA comprised a large proportion of the sequencing libraries, suggesting a significant impact on the host. Mitochondrial genes reconstructed for many of these beetles provided additional phylogenetic resolution, although the reconstruction success varied. Overall, our results demonstrate potential for reconstructing the key biological associations using sequencing data originally generated for a different purpose, highlighting a path towards comprehensive survey of interactions likely to substantially influence the population dynamics of ecologically significant species.

papers.title: A refined InDel taxonomy broadens the repertoire of mutational processes shaping multiple myeloma
papers.abstract: Somatic aberrations have been extensively characterized in multiple myeloma (MM). However, the mutational processes underlying small insertions and deletions (InDels) remain poorly understood. Here, we used a recently developed 89-channel InDel classification schema which allows differentiating mutational processes. We analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from 887 MM samples, spanning both newly diagnosed (NDMM) and relapsed/refractory disease (RRMM). We identified InDel signatures associated with replication slippage, APOBEC mutagenesis, topoisomerase 1 (TOP1)-mediated mutagenesis, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), and two rare DNA damage repair-deficiency signatures. In two randomized clinical trials, incorporation of the APOBEC InDel signature InD9a improved treatment outcome prediction as pertaining to progression-free survival (PFS) and achievement of minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity. InD29, a signature linked to NHEJ-mediated errors, was detected in both NDMM and RRMM, and was enriched in samples exhibiting melphalan-associated mutagenesis and high SV burden. Genome-wide analysis identified a recurrent InDel hotspot at TXNDC5, a highly expressed gene in MM located within a region implicated in complex genomic rearrangements, with predominantly noncoding alterations suggesting potential regulatory consequences. Finally, InDel signatures revealed the presence of mismatch-repair deficiency (MMRd) and homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) phenotypes, even in cases without germline predisposition. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive characterization of InDel mutagenesis in MM, revealing previously underexplored relationships and demonstrating potential to refine comprehensive genomic classifications of MM.

papers.title: FiberTron enables regulatory variant effect prediction and testing from multi-omic long reads of a single sample
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art sequence-to-function models are trained on large compendia of public data to predict regulatory activity across hundreds of cell types. However, they are not designed to interpret individual genomes, effects in under-sampled cell types, or provide a comprehensive view of how genetic variation influences complex diseases. Here we show that a single sample profiled with Fiber-seq and Nanopore direct RNA-seq contains enough information to train such a model from scratch. FiberTron, a 12M parameter convolutional-transformer model, takes 524 kb of reference sequence and predicts CpG methylation, chromatin accessibility and strand-specific transcript coverage at base-pair resolution (median Pearson's r of 0.85-0.97 on held-out chromosomes). Trained in under a day on a single four-GPU node, our HG002 model performs on par with models such as AlphaGenome on dsQTL and eQTL variant effect prediction tasks, despite being over an order of magnitude smaller. As training uses reference sequence only, each sample's phased multi-omic long reads remain available to test its variant-effect predictions. FiberTron recapitulates OAS1 splicing variation associated with COVID-19 risk, recovers 79% of allele-specific accessibility variants in a melanoma line, identifies oncogenic TERT promoter and TAL1 enhancer mutations, and predicts EWSR1::ATF1 fusion transcript expression and its unique chromatin imprint in a rare clear cell sarcoma patient sample. Lightweight single-sample training brings base-resolution interpretation of non-coding variation within reach of individual laboratories.

papers.title: Divergent immune trajectories distinguish resistance and susceptibility to bacterial leaf streak in wheat
papers.abstract: Bacterial leaf streak (BLS) is an increasingly important disease affecting several cereal crops. The mechanisms linking quantitative trait loci for resistance to downstream immune response against BLS in wheat remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a chromosome-scale genome assembly of the BLS resistant cultivar Boost. With de novo annotation of Boost and Timstein (susceptible cultivar) assemblies, we established a cultivar-resolved framework for dissecting BLS resistance. Both cultivars encoded highly similar immune receptor repertoires, but the major resistance locus, QBls.fcu-3B.1, comprised a divergent receptor kinase haplotype with extensive structural variations, divergent tandem receptor arrays, and constitutively elevated expression of multiple receptor kinases in the resistant cultivar. Candidate receptor kinases in Boost exhibited conserved intracellular kinase domains but substantial divergence among extracellular recognition domains relative to their syntenic homologs in Timstein. Dual reference transcriptome analyses at 24, 48, and 96 hours after inoculation (HAI) revealing contrasting immune trajectories in resistant and susceptible cultivars. Boost progressed through a focused signaling transition at 48 HAI, followed by coordinated activation of several defense modules, such as antimicrobial metabolism, cell wall reinforcement, transcriptional regulation, and immune homeostasis. In contrast, the susceptible cultivar underwent coordinated repression of these defense-related modules together with chromatin-associated transcriptional changes and induction of host transcriptional machinery during disease establishment. Our findings suggest that quantitative resistance to BLS is associated not simply with immune receptor composition, but also with constitutive immune surveillance and temporal coordination of downstream defense, providing a putative mechanistic framework linking natural genomic variations to quantitative BLS resistance in wheat.

papers.title: Pharmacogenomic diversity at tuberculosis-treatment loci across African populations: phased haplotypes, regulatory architecture and NAT2 acetylator inference
papers.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis imposes a major public-health burden in Africa, while variation in isoniazid and rifampicin disposition creates opportunities for improved pharmacotherapy. The population architecture of extended, phased pharmacogenomic backgrounds remains less well characterized than individual marker frequencies. Methods: We analyzed high-coverage, phased GRCh38 genomes from 661 unrelated individuals sampled from five continental-African and two African-diaspora populations at NAT2, SLCO1B1, CES2, HLA-B, NR1I2 and UGT1A1. We integrated frequency differentiation, reduced phased signatures, linkage disequilibrium, functional annotation and NAT2 core-allele inference with individual-clustered permutation tests. Results: The six loci contributed 17,223 annotated variant records and 276 entries in a capped frequency-differentiation register. Exact NAT2 core-definition matching was achieved for 1,321/1,322 chromosomes (99.92%), and determinate genotype-inferred acetylator categories for 620/661 individuals (93.80%). Among the sampled continental-African populations, 35-site noncore background distributions differed within NAT2 *5 (BH-adjusted q=0.000100), *4 (q=0.024733) and *6 (q=0.000350) groups. Distinct phased and linkage architectures also characterized transporter, hydrolysis, regulatory and HLA-B genomic regions. Conclusion: African population-associated variation extends beyond commonly used pharmacogenetic allele definitions. The observed NAT2 backgrounds and complementary locus signatures provide a foundation for targeted molecular studies and prospective pharmacokinetic validation that could inform future population-responsive TB treatment research.

papers.title: Diversity of Environmental and Genome-Associated Eukaryotic Circular Rep-Encoding Single-Stranded DNA Viruses
papers.abstract: Circular Rep-encoding single-stranded (CRESS) DNA viruses are widespread across diverse environments, yet their genomic diversity, evolutionary relationships, and associations with eukaryotic hosts remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the evolutionary diversity of CRESS DNA viruses by integrating replication-associated protein (Rep) sequences from environmental viral metagenomes, publicly available viral references, and endogenous viral elements (EVEs) identified in fungal and algal genomes. Genome-wide screening revealed numerous EVEs distributed across diverse fungal and algal lineages, highlighting the potential historical associations between CRESS DNA viruses and eukaryotic hosts. Phylogenetic analyses revealed considerable diversity among CRESS DNA viruses, including sequences that could not be assigned to currently recognized viral families. Yet, several of these unclassified sequences formed well-supported monophyletic clades, suggesting that existing taxonomic classifications may require further revision. Furthermore, phylogenetic relationships within and among established viral families suggest that existing taxonomic boundaries may not fully capture the evolutionary diversity of these viruses. The phylogenetic placement of fungal and algal EVEs alongside environmental and reference viral sequences further provides insights into the evolutionary relationships between CRESS DNA viruses and eukaryotic genomes. Collectively, our findings expand the known evolutionary diversity of CRESS DNA viruses, identify distinct viral lineages requiring further taxonomic evaluation, and provide a framework for investigating their genomic evolution, taxonomic relationships, and associations with eukaryotic hosts.

papers.title: BASIN: Background-Anchored Signal Normalization with Integrated Quality Control for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
papers.abstract: Quantitative comparison of CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag datasets is complicated when a perturbation changes the global abundance of the profiled chromatin feature or when there is substantial variability between replicates. Read-depth normalization removes global differences by design, whereas exogenous spike-in normalization can introduce substantial technical variability. We developed Background-Anchored SIgnal Normalization (BASIN), an endogenous-reference framework that exploits recurrent, peak-like background in IgG controls as a quantitative internal reference. BASIN Anchor Regions (BARs) act as reproducible read sinks whose representation rises as specific signal falls, allowing global differences to be inferred from the balance between specific and nonspecific reads. BASIN comprises three pipelines: OVERTURE identifies and evaluates BAR panels, HARMONY derives and applies robust sample-specific scale factors from trimmed BAR signal, and CODA determines whether the assumptions supporting normalization are satisfied. BASIN provides a validated, ready-to-use universal BAR panel for Drosophila melanogaster, and the OVERTURE pipeline enables BAR panel development in other organisms. We tested BASIN against independent expectations and compared its performance with spike-in normalization. BASIN remained quantitatively stable across a >100-fold cell-input titration and detected global depletion of H3K36me3 in Set2 mutants that read-depth normalization concealed. BASIN also preserved expected H3K9me3 differences even when target signal overlapped anchor regions. Applied to a variety of profiling experiments, CODA distinguished normalization failures arising from both biological and technical causes. BASIN thus converts reproducible background from a nuisance signal into an internal reference standard, enabling spike-in-free quantification of global chromatin changes while providing an explicit framework to test when and why that normalization can or cannot be trusted.

papers.title: A stop codon shared by all Gyps vultures, including the three Critically Endangered species of South Asia, lies in a coding exon of the bird gene CYP2C45
papers.abstract: Veterinary diclofenac devastated three South Asian Gyps vultures, but the basis of their sensitivity is unclear. A stop codon reported in a Cape vulture P450 gene, described as CYP2C19 in a retained intron, was re-examined with public data: 45 genome assemblies, raw reads of seven Gyps birds and a liver transcriptome. The gene is the bird CYP2C45, without a one-to-one human orthologue. The stop (codon 338, CGA[->]TGA) lies in coding exon 7; the intron is spliced normally, the mRNA carries the stop, and the truncated protein lacks the haem-binding cysteine. The stop was found in all eight living Gyps species, homozygous wherever testable, and in none of 27 other raptors, including two killed by diclofenac. It arose once, 1.5-10.6 million years ago on the Gyps stem, and the gene has since evolved near-neutrally. This genus-wide loss marks Gyps vulnerability but cannot explain diclofenac deaths in other raptors.

papers.title: Genomic Characterisation of the Irish Traditional BoRiabhach Cattle Breed
papers.abstract: The BoRiabhach is a highly endangered traditional landrace cattle breed in Ireland with a culturally significant history. The Irish Gaelic word "riabhach" means "streaked", "striped", or "brindled", and a distinctive brindle coat colour pattern is characteristic of the BoRiabhach breed. The breed had declined to about 20 animals by 2016 and has no systematic pedigree. Despite conservation efforts that have increased the population to an estimated 70 animals, the breed remains one of Europe's most critically endangered livestock genetic resources. We present the first genomic characterisation of the BoRiabhach breed, using Illumina BovineSNP50 genotypes of 84 BoRiabhach animals and 688 cattle from 28 European comparator breeds. Using model-based clustering, we identified a BoRiabhach-specific ancestry component. Only 28 animals carried more than 50% of this component, which we term "high-BRBH"; the remaining 56 showed extensive introgression, chiefly from Limousin and Holstein, which explains the breed's high observed heterozygosity. Phylogenetic analysis placed the high-BRBH cohort with British Shorthorn and Lincoln Red within a British-Irish clade, distinct from Kerry and Dexter, and recovered a Limousin-to-BoRiabhach migration edge. This high-BRBH core group exhibited the lowest effective population size (Ne) of any adequately sampled breed and consists of closely related animals: 34% of pairs within the core were second-degree relatives or closer. Conservation of the BoRiabhach must therefore balance breed distinctiveness with genetic diversity. We recommend genotyping all extant animals, recording genomic ancestry at registration, managing mating based on genomic relatedness as well as ancestry, and cryopreserving germplasm from the high-BRBH core population.

papers.title: Cortical neurons accumulate point mutations at similar rates in mice and humans
papers.abstract: Across vertebrate species, it has long been known that germline mutation rates per year are inversely proportional to reproductive ages. A similar pattern was recently reported in mammals for mutations in colonic epithelium, leading to speculation that this inter-species scaling may apply to many cell types. We tested whether a similar relationship holds in postmitotic cells, by estimating point mutation rates in mouse cortical neurons from PacBio HiFi circular consensus sequencing data. Our analysis revealed a significant effect of age on the number of point mutations, of 25.9 mutations per diploid genome per year (95% CI: [17.7, 34.1]). This rate is comparable to the one reported for human neurons, indicating that somatic rates need not scale with lifespan. Our findings further demonstrate that a readily available sequencing method can be used to reliably identify somatic mutations at single-cell resolution.

papers.title: Transposon-driven pervasive genome restructuring and regulatory evolution in early-diverging Holomycota
papers.abstract: Early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi showcase major evolutionary transitions in the fungal kingdom, share features with other eukaryotic clades and bacteria, and include pathogens of significant concern. These lineages contain some of the most reduced and expanded genome architectures of the fungal kingdom and have adopted unique DNA methylation systems. Yet, the evolutionary trajectory of early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi remains poorly understood. A key driver is thought to be transposable elements, which shape genomic plasticity, organization and regulation. Here, we perform a comprehensive comparative analysis across the Holomycota to chart drivers of early fungal evolution. We demonstrate that contrasting transposon dynamics directly shape genomic diversity across these lineages, fueling extensive protein domain expansions through widespread co-option. This heterogeneous landscape is regulated by a multi-layered epigenetic network impacting chromatin configuration, and we reveal a distinct transcriptional activation role for adenine methylation over specific transposons. Beyond driving functional innovation, mobile elements serve as a source of regulatory diversification, providing transcription factor binding sites at key chromosomal features. Furthermore, synteny tracking uncovers multiple whole-genome duplication events across Mucoromycotina, where DNA transposons preferentially accumulate at duplication breakpoints and undergo rapid inactivation. Strikingly, we also show that horizontal transposon transfers frequently cross deep evolutionary boundaries, including cross-kingdom exchanges with protists. Together, our findings illuminate key drivers of genome architecture in non-Dikarya fungi and reshape our understanding of genome dynamics across the fungal kingdom.
